extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, copyholders, typesetters, and publishing production staff
extracted.subtask_description: Practical style and production standards for preparing manuscripts, marking and reading proofs, and typesetting/page makeup for books and similar printed works. Covers spacing, indentation, headings, proofs, proofreading practice, copyholding, and proofreader's marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of em/en/hair spaces and dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines em as the size of the square of the current type (used as unit of measurement), en as half an em, and hair-space as any space thinner than a 5-em; defines em/en/2-em/3-em quads and corresponding dashes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct unit for spacing and dash widths (e.g., an em dash is the width of an em; an en dash the width of an en quad). Examples shown in text illustrate appearance. Treat multi-em and fractional em spaces by these definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard word and sentence spacing (Section 262, 269–273)
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard line should have a 3-em space between words not separated by other punctuation and after commas; an en quad after semicolons, and after colons followed by a lower-case letter; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; an em quad after periods and after sentence-ending exclamation and interrogation points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thin spaces after §, % and similar signs and for metric symbols; no space between currency symbols ($, £) and numerals; special spacing for scripture references and numerals at beginning of lines (en or em quads as specified). Maintain the specified proportions when increasing or decreasing spacing to justify lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing adjustment and justification rules (Sections 263–266)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reducing spacing in a line, begin with commas and letters of slanting form; to increase, begin with overlapping letters and straight-up-and-down letters; avoid abrupt changes between thin- and wide-spaced lines; never hair-space or em-quad a line to avoid a run-over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a well-spaced line with mostly 3-em spaces, ensure the remainder are at most an en quad. To justify a line, adjust spacing to make it even. Avoid following an exceptionally thin line with an exceptionally wide one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation rules by measure and type size (Section 274)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifies indentation amounts depending on measure (column width in picas) and type size: e.g., in measures <10 picas indent all sizes 1 em; in 10–20 picas different indent amounts for 11-pt., 10-pt., 9-pt., 8-pt., 6-pt., etc.; separate specifications for hanging indentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the given table of indentation values for plain paragraphs and hanging indentions. Use the prescribed em measures rather than arbitrary values to maintain typographic harmony across measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry indentation and centering (Section 275)
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry, center the longest line and govern indentation by that; if the longest line is disproportionately long, use an average of long lines. When quotations of poems vary slightly in length, indent all alike. Align blank verse and generally align consecutive rhyming lines; indent alternate rhymes alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indent according to rhyme patterns and line lengths; if a line is disproportionately short, indent it more. When multiple short poems follow, maintain consistent indentation for readability and centered appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph types and usage (Sections 276, 284)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two paragraph kinds: plain (first line indented, others flush) and hanging (first line flush, others indented). Plain paragraphs are generally preferable; hanging indention is used to bring opening words or numbers into relief or when a center-head makes more than three lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain paragraphs for ordinary reading matter; use hanging indention selectively for emphasis, lists, or long heads as indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads and slugs (Sections 277–278)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a metal strip used to separate lines; the standard lead is 2 points thick. A slug is thicker than a lead and used in make-up after headlines, with standard sizes 6 and 12 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and apply standard lead/slug sizes when specifying line spacing (leaded vs. solid set).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heads and headings layout (Sections 279–283)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines center-heads, side-heads, cul-in heads, box-heads, and running-heads, and specifies typical type treatments: center-heads often caps or small caps and pyramid or hanging indention when multiline; side-heads often set in italics with only first word capitalized; running-heads set at top of each page and recommended two sizes smaller than text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a center-head exceeds lines use inverted pyramid (2–3 lines) or hanging indention (>3 lines). Use caps/small caps/bold face as indicated, and adhere to recommended sizing for running-head legibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof types and their uses (Sections 285–289)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines galley-proof (impression in a galley), page-proof (type in page form), plate- or foundry-proof (proof before electrotype cast with black border), foul proof (galley containing author's corrections), and revise (new proof corrected from a marked proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know which proof stage is appropriate for corrections; plate corrections are expensive and likely to injure plates—avoid them when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript preparation rules (HINTS TO AUTHORS AND EDITORS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be typewritten (preferred) or perfectly clear handwriting; sheets uniform size (9" x 11" desirable); use only one side; never roll—place flat; fasten sheets only by pins or clips (use mucilage when joining pieces to avoid lost slips); leave liberal top and left margins for directions; number pages consecutively; mark inserted/omitted pages clearly; additions marked as Insert A, Insert B with insertion points indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these mechanical rules to avoid production delays and errors. Submit copy for title-pages, prefaces, contents, and indexes with the manuscript; compile index copy from special page-proofs and deliver promptly to printers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote preparation and numbering (HINTS TO AUTHORS AND EDITORS / Footnotes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes should be clearly designated and separated from the text (e.g., by a rule-line or different color ink); in text indicate footnote by a superior figure matching the note; never run footnotes into the text; number footnotes consecutively through an article or by chapters rather than restarting per page when using linotype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note linotype considerations: numbering per page is impracticable on linotype because changing a number can necessitate resetting the whole line; monotype or hand-set matter permits simple number substitution. Use consecutive numbering to avoid costly resets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading and returning proofs (Reading of Proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors/editors should read and return proofs promptly, answer all queries in proofs, and use the standard proofreader's marks (not a personal system). Remember that changes in type cost money and later stages add to cost; necessary alterations should be made at the galley-proof stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return the original manuscript with the galley-proof for reference; accompany each successive proof set with the previous marked set to facilitate calculation of alteration costs. Avoid corrections in plates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreader responsibilities and conduct (HINTS TO PROOFREADERS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofread as if you were the author; be especially careful with proper names and figures; verify doubtful copy by research or query; make queries clear and transfer manuscript queries to proofs; be discreet and avoid trivial questions; correct palpable errors regardless of copy; do not follow copy blindly; the Manual of Style is the proofreader's guide—do not defer style decisions to authors/editors; cultivate speed but prioritize accuracy; in rush situations protect yourself by noting limitations; put initials on every galley read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act as arbiter when manuscript is unclear; do not ask authors or editors to decide basic style questions covered by the Manual. Keep records of your work and initial galleys to attribute responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyholder technique and conduct (HINTS TO COPYHOLDERS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a low, soft, clear reading voice; small words are as essential as big ones; enunciate plural 's' distinctly; regulate speed and avoid racing; do not guess at words—look carefully; sit at right angles to reader; slow down when reader marks corrections; evolve simple signals (e.g., taps) for italicized words; do not waste the proofreader's time with style queries the proofreader should know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfer marks carefully (a misplaced mark can create multiple errors); arrange proofs and manuscripts neatly; ensure manuscripts accompany galleys; indicate envelope contents; fasten pins at top center, not diagonally; maintain neat proofroom records and files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard proofreader's marks (PR0OFREADER'S MARKS)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defined set of marks for common corrections: dele (delete), turn (letter reversed), put in space, close up (no space), bad spacing, wrong font, transpose, make new paragraph, indent/put in em-quad, carry left/right, elevate/depress, restore retained words, ligature printing, query to author, put in lower case, put in roman/italic/boldface, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard marks (see referenced page for full list) rather than inventing a personal system, and apply them consistently so compositors and typesetters can act without misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting machine differences and implications for corrections (Sections 293–294 and notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotype casts characters separately from perforated matrices and allows characters to be substituted without resetting entire lines; linotype casts slugs (lines) so any small change can require resetting the whole line and affect subsequent lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because linotype may necessitate resetting many lines when a single number changes, plan footnote numbering and other change-prone elements accordingly (prefer consecutive numbering through an article rather than per-page numbering on linotype matter). Favor making necessary alterations at guillotine stages that minimize resetting costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid costly late-stage corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in type at late stages (page-proof or plate) cost money and may damage plates; corrections should be avoided where possible and made earlier in galley-proof stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make manuscripts as perfect as possible before delivering to the printer; answer proof queries promptly; understand that even omission or addition of a single word may require resetting and repaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to Manual's punctuation, capitalization, and hyphenation rules (Index summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the Manual's detailed rules for capitalization (titles, proper names, institutions, epochs, etc.), punctuation (comma, colon, dash usage), abbreviations, dates, numerals, hyphenation and compounds, and other style points as enumerated in the index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the relevant sections for specific cases (e.g., comma rules §§144–162, capitalization §§1–57, dashes §§166–175, compounds 183–209). The index lists section references for particular items; use the Manual as the arbiter for style decisions rather than ad hoc choices.
